title: The Doloneia: a book apart?
greek: Δολώνεια (Doloneia)
short: An ancient note claims Book 10 was composed separately by Homer and inserted into the Iliad by Peisistratus; its place in the poem is still debated.
body: Book 10, the night raid of Odysseus and Diomedes known since antiquity as the Doloneia, has long been suspected. A scholion in the Townley manuscript (schol. T) says that the book was composed by Homer separately and not as part of the Iliad, and was placed in the poem by Peisistratus, the sixth-century tyrant of Athens. Leaf took the report seriously: no later book refers to these events, the captured horses of Rhesus never reappear (not even in the chariot race of Book 23), the night is crowded after Book 9, and the style and vocabulary are unusual, with many Odyssean words. Bryan Hainsworth's Cambridge commentary treats the book's problems at length. Since the 1990s scholars such as Casey Dué and Mary Ebbott have defended it as a skilled example of a traditional theme, the ambush (lochos), a kind of night warfare with its own values; Nagy argues that the night setting itself explains its separateness. Read with Book 9, it shows the Achaeans recovering their nerve by cunning after the failure of persuasion.

anchor: the wide mouth of bitter war
title: Zeus' lightning and the 'mouth of war'
greek: πτολέμοιο μέγα στόμα πευκεδανοῖο (ptolemoio mega stoma peukedanoio)
short: Agamemnon's groans come as often as Zeus' lightning flashes before rain, hail, snow or 'the great mouth of bitter war': a weather simile that ends in war.
body: The simile compares the frequency of Agamemnon's groans to the repeated flashes of lightning sent by 'the husband of fair-haired Hera' when he prepares a storm. The list of what the lightning may announce, rain, hail, snow, ends unexpectedly with 'the great mouth of war'. Leaf, who disliked this book's style, objected that the simile treats war as if it were a natural phenomenon like a snowstorm, and suggested the poet meant lightning without rain as an omen of war; he calls the passage an 'incompetent piece of expression'. A more sympathetic reading sees the surprise as the point: in Agamemnon's anxious mind every sign from Zeus foretells battle. The rare adjective peukedanos, 'bitter' (perhaps 'piercing'), is of uncertain sense, and stoma, 'mouth' or 'front', is used of the front line of battle in later Greek (Leaf cites the tragedy Rhesus, line 491, and suggests the image began as the jaws of a beast closing on whatever lies between two armies).

title: Tearing out the hair to Zeus
greek: πολλὰς ἐκ κεφαλῆς προθελύμνους ἕλκετο χαίτας ὑψόθ' ἐόντι Διί (pollas ek kephalēs prothelumnous helketo chaitas)
short: Agamemnon pulls out his hair 'by the roots' as an appeal to Zeus above: a gesture of extreme grief normally used in mourning for the dead.
body: Tearing the hair is a standard Homeric sign of grief: Priam tears his white hair as he begs Hector to come inside the walls (22.77-8), and Achilles fouls and pulls his hair at the news of Patroclus' death (18.23-7). Here the gesture is made by a living commander for an army not yet lost, and it is directed 'to Zeus who is on high'. Leaf lists 'tearing out the hair to Zeus' among the unusual expressions of the book and notes the exaggeration in prothelumnous, 'by the roots' (the same word describes trees uprooted by the boar in 9.541). Whether one reads it as overstatement or as a deliberate picture of Agamemnon's panic, it continues his despair from the start of Book 9 and contrasts with the confidence of the night raid that follows.

title: Heroes dressed in animal skins
greek: δέρμα λέοντος αἴθωνος μεγάλοιο ποδηνεκές (derma leontos aithōnos megaloio podēnekes)
short: Agamemnon and Diomedes put on lion skins, Menelaus a leopard's, Dolon a wolf's with a marten-skin cap: night warfare has its own costume.
body: Book 10 is unusually interested in dress. Agamemnon wraps himself in the skin of a 'tawny, great lion, reaching to his feet'; Menelaus takes a leopard's dappled hide (10.29-30); Diomedes the same lion skin (10.177-8); the Trojan scout Dolon a grey wolf's skin and a cap of marten (10.334-5). Elsewhere in the Iliad only Paris wears a leopard skin (3.17), marking him as a lightly armed archer. Leaf noted these skins among the signs of the book's distinctive character and reported the suggestion that they resemble the lion skin of Heracles, a feature introduced into art and poetry in the seventh century. Dué and Ebbott read them instead as part of the traditional equipment of ambush: warriors who fight at night by stealth take on the nature of predators, and the animal imagery of the similes (dogs, lions, hounds) matches the costume. The skins also prepare for Dolon, whose wolf skin turns him into the hunted prey.

title: Ambrosial night
greek: νύκτα δι' ἀμβροσίην (nukta di' ambrosiēn)
short: Murray's 'immortal night' renders ambrosiē, 'ambrosial, divine': night belongs to the gods, a time when mortal action is uncanny and dangerous.
body: Ambrosios is the adjective of ambrosia, the food of the gods; its root means 'immortal' (a- 'not' + brotos 'mortal'). Homer applies it to divine hair, garments, sandals and oil, and to night and sleep, which come from the gods and are not under human control. Murray renders the phrase 'immortal night' here (in Book 2 he wrote 'ambrosial night' for the same Greek). In Book 10 the phrase matters because the whole action takes place in the dark: Menelaus fears that no one will dare to go out alone 'through the ambrosial night' to spy, and Odysseus later asks why the leaders are wandering through it (10.142). Night in the Iliad normally stops fighting (7.282, 8.502); the Doloneia is the exception, a night raid in which the usual rules of open combat are suspended.

anchor: calling each man by his lineage
title: Calling men by their father's name
greek: πατρόθεν ἐκ γενεῆς ὀνομάζων ἄνδρα ἕκαστον (patrothen ek geneēs onomazōn andra hekaston)
short: Agamemnon tells Menelaus to wake each man by his patronymic and family name, 'giving honour to each', and not to be too proud for a herald's work.
body: Leaf explains that patrothen ek geneēs forms a single phrase, 'by his father's, that is, his family name', and that the poem follows the instruction: men are addressed as 'son of Tydeus', 'son of Laertes', 'son of Neleus' (10.87, 144, 159). To use a man's patronymic and full title, such as 'Zeus-born' or 'great glory of the Achaeans', is to honour him; Leaf glosses kudainōn as 'using the full complimentary title'. Agamemnon adds 'do not be proud', that is, do not think yourself too great to act as a herald, 'but let us toil ourselves'. Coming after Book 9, the scene shows the king attempting the courtesy that he failed to show Achilles. The custom of naming by the father is also the basis of epithets such as 'Atreides' and 'Peleides' throughout the poem.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 10.68-69

title: Nestor's purple cloak (chlaina)
greek: χλαῖναν ... φοινικόεσσαν διπλῆν ἐκταδίην, οὔλη δ' ἐπενήνοθε λάχνη
short: The chlaina was a woollen cloak worn doubled and fastened with a pin; it could be spread out as a blanket at night.
body: Nestor, roused by Agamemnon, dresses as for a cold night: tunic, sandals, and a chlaina, 'purple, double, wide-spreading, with thick wool on it'. Leaf explains that the mantle, like a Scottish plaid, was usually worn folded double around the body but could be spread out (ektadiē) to cover a man as a coverlet; diplē, 'double', is found again only in the description of Odysseus' purple cloak at Odyssey 19.225-6, where it is fastened with a famous golden brooch. Leaf also notes that the adjective phoinikoessa is a late form. Purple dye was costly, and the colour marks Nestor's rank even on a night errand. The detail is typical of the book's fondness for describing dress and arms in each arming scene: Agamemnon, Menelaus, Nestor, Odysseus and Diomedes each put on something different.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 10.133-134

title: Spears planted on their butt-spikes (saurōtēr)
greek: ἔγχεα δέ σφιν ὄρθ' ἐπὶ σαυρωτῆρος ἐλήλατο (enchea de sphin orth' epi saurōtēros elēlato)
short: Diomedes' men sleep with spears stuck upright in the ground on their bronze butt-spikes; Aristotle used this line to show that Homer describes old customs.
body: The saurōtēr (literally 'lizard-killer') was the metal spike on the butt end of a spear, which allowed it to be planted in the ground and served as a second point if the head broke. The word occurs only here in the Iliad. Aristotle, discussing objections critics raised against Homer, quotes the line in Poetics 25 and answers that it describes the custom of the time, which, he says, the Illyrians still follow. The picture is vivid: the bronze of the planted spears 'shone far like the lightning of father Zeus', while Diomedes himself sleeps on an ox-hide with a rug under his head, his comrades using their shields as pillows. Nestor wakes him by nudging him with his foot, a moment of easy familiarity between the old and the young warrior.

title: On a razor's edge
greek: νῦν γὰρ δὴ πάντεσσιν ἐπὶ ξυροῦ ἵσταται ἀκμῆς (epi xurou histatai akmēs)
short: Nestor says the Achaeans' fate 'stands on the edge of a razor', ruin or survival: the earliest instance of a proverb that passed into Greek and English.
body: Nestor tells Diomedes that 'now for all of us it stands on a razor's edge', either grim destruction for the Achaeans or life. Leaf explains the image as balancing on an edge so thin that a fall to one side or the other must soon happen, and notes that neither xuron, 'razor', nor akmē, 'edge', occurs elsewhere in Homer; razors were nevertheless known from the Bronze Age, and Mycenaean men shaved the upper lip. The phrase became proverbial: in Herodotus, Dionysius of Phocaea tells the Ionians before the battle of Lade that 'our affairs stand on a razor's edge' (6.11); Theognis uses it (557), and Sophocles' Teiresias tells Creon that he now stands 'on the razor of fortune' (Antigone 996). It survives in English through translations of these passages.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 10.173-174

Sophocles, Antigone 996

anchor: even as dogs keep painful watch
title: Simile of the watchdogs
greek: ὡς δὲ κύνες περὶ μῆλα δυσωρήσωνται ἐν αὐλῇ (hōs de kunes peri mēla dusōrēsōntai en aulēi)
short: The sentinels stay awake like sheepdogs that hear a wild beast coming down through the woods: the first of the book's many animal similes.
body: The sentries are compared to dogs that 'keep wretched watch' (dusōreō, a word found only here) over sheep in a fold when they hear a fierce beast coming through the forest in the hills, with an uproar of men and dogs around it, 'and sleep is lost to them'. The simile fits the situation precisely: the Achaeans are the flock, their guards are the dogs, and the Trojans camped on the plain are the predator. Leaf's note concerns the unusual verb form, which he regards as a rare survival of an old subjunctive. Herding and hunting similes are among the commonest in Homer; Steven Lonsdale's study shows how they place men in the roles of predator, prey and protector. Book 10 is full of them: dogs here, two lions (10.297), two hounds hunting a fawn or hare (10.360-4), a lion among unguarded flocks (10.485-6).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 10.183

title: The reward: a black ewe from every chief
greek: οἶν ... μέλαιναν θῆλυν ὑπόρρηνον (oin melainan thēlun hupornēnon)
short: Nestor promises the volunteer spy great fame, a black ewe with her lamb from every leader, and a place at all feasts; Leaf thought the reward absurdly small.
body: Nestor's offer has two parts, a gift (dosis) and fame (kleos): 'great would his fame be under heaven among all men'. Each chief will give 'a black ewe with a lamb beneath her', 'and no possession is equal to it', and he will always be present at feasts and drinking. Leaf found the material reward ridiculous for chiefs rich in gold and slaves and suspected that the author wanted a touch of heroic simplicity. He reports, however, a suggestion of Peppmüller that line 217 means 'he will be present in the songs sung at feasts', that is, celebrated in poetry, comparing Theognis 237-54, where the poet promises Cyrnus that he will be sung at every banquet. Read that way, the reward matches the theme of kleos so prominent in Book 9. It also anticipates Hector's promise to Dolon, who asks for Achilles' horses as his reward (10.321-3, 10.329-31), a prize he never receives.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 10.214-217
Theognis 237-254 (the poet's promise of fame at feasts)

title: 'When two go together'
greek: σύν τε δύ' ἐρχομένω, καί τε πρὸ ὃ τοῦ ἐνόησεν (sun te du' erchomenō, kai te pro ho tou enoēsen)
short: Diomedes' reason for wanting a companion, 'when two go together, one sees before the other', became a proverb quoted by Plato and Aristotle.
body: Diomedes volunteers but asks for a partner: when two go together, one notices before the other how there may be profit, while a man alone has a shorter wit and slighter plan. Nagy stresses the verb noeō: Diomedes means taking the initiative through perception, the quality for which he will choose Odysseus. The lines became proverbial. In Plato's Symposium (174d) Socrates quotes 'two going together' to Aristodemus as they walk uninvited to Agathon's dinner, and in the Protagoras (348d) to invite a joint search for truth; Aristotle cites the line in the Nicomachean Ethics (8.1, 1155a) to show the value of friendship. Leaf notes the remarkable sixfold repetition of te in three lines, a mark of old correlative usage. The pairing of Diomedes and Odysseus, strength and cunning, is the basis of the whole raid.

anchor: not though one be more kingly
title: Choosing the best, not the most kingly
greek: μηδ' ἐς γενεὴν ὁρόων, μηδ' εἰ βασιλεύτερός ἐστιν (mēd' es geneēn horoōn, mēd' ei basileuteros estin)
short: Agamemnon tells Diomedes to choose the best man, not the 'more kingly' one, secretly fearing he will pick Menelaus; the advice echoes his own claim in Book 9.
body: Many volunteer: the two Aiantes, Meriones, Nestor's son, Menelaus and Odysseus. Agamemnon urges Diomedes not to leave the better man behind out of respect (aidōs) and take a worse one, 'looking to birth, not even if he is more kingly'. The narrator explains his motive: he feared for fair-haired Menelaus. Nagy points out the irony: in Book 9 Agamemnon demanded that Achilles yield to him because he was basileuteros, 'more kingly' (9.160); now he states the opposite principle, that merit should count above rank, when it suits him. Diomedes chooses Odysseus for his intelligence and because Athena loves him, and Odysseus answers modestly, asking neither praise nor blame from men who already know him. The episode shows the Achaean leaders cooperating, in contrast to the quarrel that dominates Books 1 and 9.

sources.cite: Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Iliad Rhapsody 10', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2016, rev. 2018, comment on I.10.233-240

anchor: more than two watches have past
title: The watches of the night
greek: παρῴχηκεν δὲ πλέων νὺξ τῶν δύο μοιράων, τριτάτη δ' ἔτι μοῖρα λέλειπται
short: Odysseus says that the stars have moved on and 'more than two parts' of the night are gone, a third remaining: a puzzle already discussed by Aristotle.
body: Homeric Greeks divided the night into three parts (moirai), and telling time by the movement of the stars is an expert's skill (compare Odyssey 12.312). The line posed an ancient arithmetical problem: if more than two-thirds of the night have gone, how can a whole third remain? Aristotle, in Poetics 25, cites it as an example of ambiguity solved by reading pleōn as 'the full' two parts. Leaf records the ancient debate (10.253 was rejected by the Alexandrian editors) and answers more simply that the words mean only that nothing but the third watch is left 'for us to act in', not that it is entirely intact. Either way, the remark marks the urgency of the mission: the raid must be done before dawn, and the whole of Book 10 takes place in the last third of the same night that began in Book 8.

sources.cite: Aristotle, Poetics 25, 1461a (on 'more than two parts of the night')

title: The boar's-tusk helmet
greek: κυνέη ῥινοῦ ποιητή ... λευκοὶ δ' ὀδόντες ἀργιόδοντος ὑὸς (kuneē rhinou poiētē ... leukoi d' odontes argiodontos huos)
short: Meriones gives Odysseus a leather helmet covered with rows of boar's tusks: a real Mycenaean type, known from Bronze Age finds, preserved in epic memory.
body: The helmet is made of hide, held taut inside by many thongs, lined with felt, and covered outside with 'the white teeth of a gleaming-tusked boar, set thick on this side and that'. Leaf, writing before the major finds, tentatively read it as three layers: a leather cap padded with felt, thongs wound round it, and an outer covering of tusks. Archaeology has since shown that such helmets were common in Mycenaean Greece in the sixteenth to thirteenth centuries BCE: fragments of tusk plates have been found in many tombs, at Dendra among others, and ivory carvings show warriors wearing them. Each helmet needed the tusks of many boars, so it was a costly, aristocratic object and naturally an heirloom. H. L. Lorimer's Homer and the Monuments treated it as one of the clearest Bronze Age survivals in Homer. Its presence in a poem composed centuries later shows how oral tradition could preserve the description of objects no longer in use. Diomedes' 'skull-cap' (kataitux) of bull's hide is described at 10.257-9.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 10.263-265
H. L. Lorimer, Homer and the Monuments, London: Macmillan, 1950, ch. on helmets

title: Autolycus and the helmet's history
greek: Αὐτόλυκος (Autolukos); Ἀμύντωρ Ὀρμενίδης (Amuntōr Ormenidēs)
short: The helmet's pedigree runs from Autolycus, Odysseus' thieving grandfather, who stole it from Amyntor's house, through Amphidamas and Molus to Meriones and now to Odysseus.
body: Homer often gives a precious object a biography, as with Agamemnon's sceptre (2.101-8). This helmet was stolen by Autolycus from the house of Amyntor, son of Ormenus, at Eleon; Autolycus gave it to Amphidamas of Cythera, who gave it as a guest-gift to Molus, who gave it to his son Meriones. Two links are significant. Autolycus is Odysseus' maternal grandfather, famous in the Odyssey as the man who 'surpassed all men in thievery and oaths' (Od. 19.395-6); Leaf notes that later legend made him a son of Hermes. So the helmet returns, by gift, to the family of the thief, on a night of stealth. And Amyntor, son of Ormenus, is Phoenix's father from Book 9 (9.448); Leaf comments on the shifting location of his home, here at Eleon in Boeotia, there in Thessaly. The chain of owners also shows guest-friendship (xenia) passing valuable objects between households.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 10.266-267

title: The heron omen
greek: ἐρῳδιός (erōidios)
short: Athena sends a heron on the right; the two heroes cannot see it in the dark but hear its cry, and Odysseus takes it as a good omen.
body: Birds on the right were favourable omens in Greek divination. The bird here, erōidios, may be the night heron (Ardea nycticorax), which Leaf, following D'Arcy Thompson, notes is common in the Troad and suits a night scene; the ancient reader Zopyrus even proposed reading pellon, 'grey' (heron), for 'Pallas' in the next line. Leaf adds that the heron is a symbol of Athena on coins of Ambracia and Corinth and is treated as a bird of good omen by Aelian, Plutarch and Pliny. The fact that the omen is heard rather than seen fits the setting of the whole book. Odysseus answers with a prayer to Athena that stresses her constant presence at his side, and Diomedes follows with his own, recalling his father Tydeus' embassy to Thebes; the pair of prayers matches the pair of heroes.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 10.274
Homer, Iliad 10.274 (Greek text, ed. Murray)

anchor: nor am I unseen of thee
title: Athena and Odysseus
greek: οὐδέ σε λήθω κινύμενος (oude se lēthō kinumenos)
short: Odysseus prays to Athena as the goddess who stands by him in all his toils and sees every move he makes: the intimate bond that dominates the Odyssey.
body: In the Iliad Athena helps many Achaeans, Diomedes above all in Book 5, but this prayer describes a personal, constant relationship: 'you always stand beside me in all my toils, and I do not escape your notice when I move'. Leaf observed that this close relation of Athena to Odysseus is not elsewhere recognised in the Iliad in this form and suggested the author had the Odyssey in mind; several lines of the book have exact parallels there. Nagy connects the bond with mētis, the cunning intelligence that Athena personifies and that Odysseus embodies, and notes the opposition between Athena and Hector, whose plans she will frustrate. Diomedes was chosen precisely because 'Pallas Athena loves' Odysseus (10.245). Athena answers both men: she puts strength into Diomedes and warns him when it is time to leave (10.509-11).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1, London: Macmillan, 1900, introduction to Book X
Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Iliad Rhapsody 10', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2016, rev. 2018, comment on I.10.043-052 and I.10.241-247
Homer, Odyssey 13.299-302 (Athena on her bond with Odysseus)

title: A heifer with gilded horns
greek: βοῦν ἤνιν εὐρυμέτωπον ἀδμήτην ... χρυσὸν κέρασιν περιχεύας (boun ēnin eurumetōpon admētēn)
short: Diomedes vows Athena an unbroken yearling heifer with gold-covered horns; the same three lines are Nestor's vow in Odyssey 3.
body: A vow (euchē) promised the god a gift in return for help. The best victim was an animal never put under the yoke (admētē), that is, unused by men, and gilding the horns made the offering splendid. The three lines are repeated exactly by Nestor at Odyssey 3.382-4, and there the poet describes the whole ritual: the goldsmith Laerces is summoned to beat out the gold and wrap the horns 'so that the goddess might rejoice at the sight' (Od. 3.425-38). Leaf lists this among the many close links between Book 10 and the Odyssey. Diomedes' prayer, unlike Odysseus', rests on family history: Athena stood by his father Tydeus when he went alone as an envoy to Thebes (compare 4.384-98, 5.800-8), and he asks the same favour now.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1, London: Macmillan, 1900, introduction to Book X
Homer, Odyssey 3.382-4 (the same vow by Nestor)
Homer, Odyssey 3.425-38 (the gilding of the horns)

title: Two lions in the night
greek: βάν ῥ' ἴμεν ὥς τε λέοντε δύω διὰ νύκτα μέλαιναν (ban rh' imen hōs te leonte duō dia nukta melainan)
short: The two heroes go out like a pair of lions through the black night; later Diomedes falls on the sleeping Thracians like a lion on unguarded flocks.
body: The lion is Homer's commonest image of the attacking warrior, usually alone and hungry, often driven off by herdsmen and dogs. Here the dual leonte duō makes the pair a single predator team, and the setting, 'amid the slaughter, amid the corpses, through the armour and the black blood', recalls the battlefield of Book 8. The image returns when Diomedes kills the sleeping Thracians: 'as a lion coming upon flocks without a shepherd, goats or sheep, leaps on them with evil intent' (10.485-6). In Lonsdale's analysis, lion and herding similes structure the Iliad's battle narrative as a contest between predator and protector; in Book 10 the protectors fail, because the herdsmen are asleep. The heroes are also wearing lion skins, so simile and costume reinforce each other.

title: Hector's 'idle' oath on the staff
greek: ὣς φάτο καί ῥ' ἐπίορκον ἐπώμοσε (hōs phato kai rh' epiorkon epōmose)
short: Hector swears by Zeus on his staff that Dolon shall have Achilles' horses; the narrator calls the oath epiorkon, 'false', because it will not be fulfilled.
body: Dolon asks Hector to 'lift up the staff' (skēptron) and swear; to swear holding a sceptre, the sign of authority, is a solemn act (compare Achilles' oath on the sceptre at 1.234-44). Hector calls Zeus as witness that no other Trojan will mount Achilles' horses. The narrator comments that he swore an epiorkon oath. Elsewhere epiorkos means a perjured or broken oath, and Leaf discusses whether the verb should be epōmose, 'swore in addition', or apōmose, 'swore a negative oath'. He insists, in a later note, that Hector intends to keep his promise: the oath is 'false' only in the sense that it proves untrue, since Dolon will die. Murray's 'idle' expresses this nuance. The motif of a prize promised and never received links Dolon with Meleager in Book 9 and the black ewes of 10.215.

title: Dolon, the Trojan spy
greek: Δόλων Εὐμήδεος υἱός (Dolōn Eumēdeos huios)
short: Dolon, 'the trickster', son of the herald Eumedes, rich, ugly but swift-footed, volunteers to spy on the Greek ships in a wolf-skin and is caught and killed.
body: His name is built on dolos, 'trick, stratagem', so 'Dolon' is a speaking name for a scout; his father's name, Eumedes, means 'of good counsel', fittingly for a herald. Homer gives him a sharply drawn character: 'ill-favoured to look on, but swift of foot', rich in gold and bronze, an only brother among five sisters. Nagy notes that, apart from Dolon, the only Iliadic hero given the epithet podōkēs, 'swift-footed', and related epithets is Achilles, so Dolon is a kind of anti-Achilles, aspiring to Achilles' own horses. He wears a grey wolf skin and a cap of marten or polecat fur (ktideē kuneē; Leaf explains the animal). Louis Gernet's essay 'Dolon le loup' (1936) related this disguise to traditions of wolf-warriors and initiatory night raids; Dué and Ebbott read the wolf as a figure of ambush. The story was popular in later art and in the tragedy Rhesus attributed to Euripides, in which Dolon has a speaking part.

title: As far as mules plough
greek: ὅσσον τ' ἐπὶ οὖρα πέλονται ἡμιόνων (hosson t' epi oura pelontai hēmionōn)
short: A farming measure of distance: the width of land a team of mules ploughs in a day's work, wider than oxen manage, since mules are faster.
body: Homer measures distance here, as elsewhere, by an everyday standard: the oura of mules, the side-limits of the strip a pair of mules ploughs. Leaf explains the reasoning in detail. The furrow was of standard length in the common field, and the unit of area was a day's ploughing; mules, being faster than oxen 'at drawing the jointed plough through deep fallow', cover a wider strip in a day, so 'the range of mules' became a fixed measure, used again in the Odyssey's footrace (Od. 8.124). Leaf compares the English local measure 'daymath'. The comparison brings the world of peace into the night raid at the moment when Odysseus and Diomedes let Dolon pass before springing up behind him; the reader of the shield of Achilles (18.541-9) will recognise the ploughing scene.

title: Two hounds chasing a fawn or hare
greek: ὡς δ' ὅτε καρχαρόδοντε δύω κύνε εἰδότε θήρης (hōs d' hote karcharodonte duō kune eidote thērēs)
short: Diomedes and Odysseus cut Dolon off like two trained hounds pressing a doe or hare that runs screaming ahead of them: the spy has become the prey.
body: Again the dual: 'two sharp-toothed dogs, skilled in the hunt'. The simile completes a reversal that the costume prepared: Dolon, dressed as a wolf, is hunted like a hare or a young deer, and the hunting language continues as the heroes 'cut him off' from the Trojan host and drive him toward the ships. Hunting similes, as Lonsdale shows, often describe a warrior fleeing in panic. Athena then 'put strength' into Diomedes so that no other Achaean could claim the first blow. Diomedes deliberately throws his spear wide over Dolon's right shoulder to stop him; the terrified man stands stammering, 'his teeth chattering in his mouth', pale with fear, one of the most physically exact descriptions of terror in the poem.

title: Ransom: 'take me alive'
greek: ζωγρεῖτ', αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἐμὲ λύσομαι (zōgreit', autar egōn eme lusomai)
short: Dolon begs to be taken alive and ransomed with bronze, gold and iron; earlier in the war captives were often sold or ransomed, but now mercy is rare.
body: Zōgreō means 'take alive' (from zōos, 'alive', and agreō, 'catch'); the captive then 'ransoms himself' through his family's payment (lusomai, from luō, 'release'). The appeal uses a fixed formula: the same words are spoken by Adrastus to Menelaus (6.46-50) and by the sons of Antimachus to Agamemnon (11.131-5), and in both cases the plea is refused. Achilles reminds Lycaon that before Patroclus died he used to spare and sell captives (21.99-102). Odysseus at first reassures Dolon, 'let not death be in your thoughts', which proves to be a deceptive answer, typical of the book's world of tricks. The pattern makes Dolon's death part of the hardening of the war: ransom is offered and rejected, as Achilles will reject it from Lycaon and, at first, for Hector's body.

title: Supplication cut short
greek: ὁ μέν μιν ἔμελλε γενείου χειρὶ παχείῃ ἁψάμενος λίσσεσθαι (geneiou cheiri ... hapsamenos lissesthai)
short: Dolon is about to touch Diomedes' chin, the formal gesture of a suppliant, when Diomedes cuts off his head in mid-speech.
body: Formal supplication (hiketeia) in Homer involved physical contact: the suppliant clasped the knees and touched the chin of the person entreated, as Thetis does with Zeus (1.500-1). John Gould showed that full contact placed the suppliant under religious protection, so that rejecting him became a serious matter; Diomedes forestalls the gesture before it is complete. His reasoning is practical: released, Dolon would come back to spy or fight again. The killing is shockingly quick: 'his head, still speaking, was mingled with the dust', a line repeated in the Odyssey when Odysseus kills the suppliant Leodes (Od. 22.329). Odysseus' earlier promise ('let not death be in your thoughts') is thus revealed as a ruse. The scene is a stark example of the different ethics of night raiding, where the formal courtesies of daytime combat give way to deception.

title: The tomb of Ilus
greek: θείου παρὰ σήματι Ἴλου (theiou para sēmati Ilou)
short: Hector holds his council at the burial mound of Ilus, founder of Ilios and grandfather of Priam, a landmark in the middle of the Trojan plain.
body: Ilus, son of Tros, was Priam's grandfather and the founder from whom Ilios takes its name (genealogy at 20.230-7). His tomb (sēma) is a recurring landmark: Paris shoots Diomedes from behind it (11.371-2), the Achaeans are routed past it (11.166), and Priam passes it on his way to Achilles (24.349). Leaf notes that its position cannot be fixed beyond 'somewhere in the middle of the plain'. Hector holding council 'away from the uproar' at his ancestor's grave has more than geographical point: Nagy suggests that the setting connects Hector's planning with the cult hero Ilus, as if the Trojan leader drew counsel from the founder. Dolon's information, which Odysseus extracts here, gives the Achaeans the layout of the enemy camp and leads them to Rhesus.

title: The Trojan allies' camp
greek: Κᾶρες καὶ Παίονες ... καὶ Λέλεγες καὶ Καύκωνες δῖοί τε Πελασγοί
short: Dolon gives a short catalogue of the allied contingents and where they sleep; the Leleges and Caucones, absent from the Trojan Catalogue of Book 2, appear here.
body: Towards the sea lie the Carians, the Paeonians with their curved bows, the Leleges, the Caucones and the Pelasgians; towards Thymbre the Lycians, Mysians, Phrygians and Maeonians. Leaf observes that the list is a fairly complete roster of the peoples whom later Greek tradition regarded as the early population of mainland Greece and the coasts of Asia Minor. The Leleges and Caucones do not occur in the Catalogue of Book 2 but appear elsewhere in the poem as neighbours of the Troad (Leaf cites 20.96 and 20.329; Altes is 'king of the Leleges' at 21.86); there are other Caucones in Elis in the Odyssey (3.366). Thymbre, a town on the Scamander, is not mentioned again in Homer, although later its temple of Thymbraean Apollo was famous. Dolon's point is that the newly arrived Thracians lie apart and unguarded, an easy target.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 10.428-434

title: Rhesus, king of the Thracians
greek: Ῥῆσος Ἠϊονῆος (Rhēsos Ēïonēos)
short: The newly arrived Thracian king, with snow-white horses and golden armour; a later tradition made him invincible once his horses drank from the Scamander.
body: Dolon describes Rhesus' horses and his chariot of gold and silver, armour fit for gods rather than men. Leaf notes that the tragedy Rhesus makes him the son of the river Strymon and a Muse, which suggests a local Thracian divinity, and that his Homeric father Eioneus is probably a river name as well (there was a town Eion on the Strymon). The ancient scholia on 10.435 preserve fuller stories. According to one, an oracle said that if Rhesus and his horses once drank from the Scamander they would be invincible, which is why he was killed on his first night; Virgil seems to know this version: on the temple at Carthage Aeneas sees the horses driven off before they could taste Trojan fodder or drink the Xanthus (Aeneid 1.469-73). Another, attributed by the scholia to Pindar, says Rhesus fought gloriously for one day before Diomedes killed him. Homer tells neither; for him Rhesus is simply a rich new ally, and the prize is his horses.

title: Diomedes as an evil dream
greek: κακὸν γὰρ ὄναρ κεφαλῆφιν ἐπέστη τὴν νύκτ', Οἰνεΐδαο πάϊς, διὰ μῆτιν Ἀθήνης
short: Rhesus dies gasping, for 'an evil dream stood over his head that night, the son of Oeneus' son': Diomedes himself is the nightmare. Aristarchus rejected the second line.
body: Dreams in Homer typically 'stand over the head' of the sleeper (as the Dream sent to Agamemnon does at 2.20). The passage can be read in two ways. Either Rhesus is breathing heavily because he is having an ominous dream that fails to save him, or, with bitter irony, the 'evil dream' is Diomedes, 'the son of Oeneus' son' (that is, of Tydeus), standing over him in the dark. Leaf preferred the first sense and explains that some rhapsode, taking the phrase as a metaphor for Diomedes, added line 497 to make it explicit; that line was athetised by Aristarchus and omitted by Zenodotus. Modern readers often enjoy the metaphor, which Murray's 'like to an evil dream' preserves. The tragedy Rhesus develops the dream differently: Rhesus' charioteer dreams of two wolves leaping on the horses.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Books I-XII), London: Macmillan, 1900, note on 10.496-497

title: Washing in the sea and the bath
greek: ἐς ἀσαμίνθους βάντες ἐϋξέστας λούσαντο (es asaminthous bantes euxestas lousanto)
short: Back at the camp the heroes wash off sweat in the sea, then bathe in polished tubs (asaminthoi), anoint themselves, and pour a libation to Athena: an Odyssean close.
body: The ending follows a familiar sequence of return and refreshment: sea-washing, bath, olive oil, meal and libation. The word asaminthos, a bathtub, is common in the Odyssey (for example 3.468 and 4.48) but appears only here in the Iliad, and Leaf lists it among the words that link Book 10 with the Odyssey. Before bathing, Odysseus sets Dolon's bloody spoils on the stern of his ship 'until they should prepare a sacred offering to Athena', fulfilling the promise he made when he held them aloft (10.460-4). The horses of Rhesus are tied at the manger with Diomedes' own team. The calm domestic ending contrasts with the slaughter just narrated and closes a night that began with Agamemnon unable to sleep.
